title: Ice storm
tldr: Avoid travel on icy roads and keep away from ice-laden trees and power lines. Prepare for a long outage using safe heat and battery lights. Stay indoors until conditions improve unless your shelter is unsafe.
steps: Even thin ice can make roads and sidewalks unsafe.
Stay clear of branches, wires and roofs shedding ice.
Keep combustion equipment outdoors and maintain working CO alarms.
Plan safe transport to a warm location if heat or essential medical power fails.
next: Use footwear with traction for necessary movement and do not enter areas beneath damaged trees.
watch: Never touch or approach a fallen wire, even if it appears inactive.
review_status: source-linked editorial review; not independent expert certification
without_help: Preserve heat in a dry room, keep lights battery powered and avoid unnecessary travel. If you must move because of dangerous cold, do it before people become weak and use a route you know is passable; a car is not reliable shelter if exhaust or roads are blocked.
household: Account for children, older people, pets and anyone who needs assistance before moving. Keep shoes, medicines and a torch in the shelter area. Decide who helps whom and who carries the essential supplies; do not send a lone child to retrieve items. For this situation, brief every person on the first action: postpone travel. Agree who will manage children, pets or mobility needs while that action happens. Never touch or approach a fallen wire, even if it appears inactive.
pack_now: For ice storm, prioritize only items needed for the first action and the fallback: Preserve heat in a dry room, keep lights battery powered and avoid unnecessary travel. If you must move because of dangerous cold, do it before people become weak and use a route you know is passable; a car is not reliable shelter if exhaust or roads are blocked. Keep the relevant checklist and contact information within reach. Equipment retrieval must not delay the protective step.
scope: Civilian educational guidance. Linked references may use U.S. emergency systems; local warning methods, laws, services and conditions differ.
